excerpt: Practical criteria, common mistakes and useful decisions for this cross stitch question.
content_html:
Start from the physical size you want rather than an arbitrary color count. A 70-by-70-stitch portrait cannot use the same subtle palette as a 250-by-250 chart because resolution limits how many transitions have meaning.

This guide resolves the situation with practical criteria and avoids automatic fixes that can make the project worse or add unnecessary work.

Start from the design goal

Build structure before detail

Classify each shade by job: background, main mass, shadow, highlight, transition or accent. If two skeins perform exactly the same job and are barely distinguishable in context, one may be removable.

Control colors and symbols

Reduce the palette by looking at value as well as hue. A grayscale preview can reveal several different colors with nearly identical lightness that add little extra depth.

Check at real scale

Photo converters tend to create colors used for only a handful of stitches. Review those shades and decide whether they define an eye, edge or genuine highlight, or are noise that can merge into a neighbor.

Avoid complexity without benefit

Test several palettes at stitched scale rather than screen scale. A 35-color version may preserve forms better than a 70-color version if the larger palette mainly creates confetti.

What the PDF should make clear

In the PDF, a controlled palette simplifies supplies, key and stitching. Do not impose an arbitrary maximum: the right number is the smallest palette that preserves the visual intention.

Overall, the best solution preserves stability, readability and a reasonable stitching experience. Our editorial content should explain why, and our patterns should apply the same judgment to materials, layout and working notes.

The right number of colors is the smallest palette that preserves the subject at the intended stitch size. More colors do not automatically mean more realism. If two shades occupy tiny scattered areas and look identical from normal viewing distance, combining them can reduce thread changes without sacrificing the image.

Start with value structure: light, midtone and dark areas should define the form before subtle hue differences are added. In a portrait, the eyes, nose and major facial planes may need protected transitions; in a flat graphic, five strong colors may be more effective than twenty. Palette decisions should follow the visual job each color performs.

Finished dimensions matter because a larger chart can support more gradual transitions. At 200 stitches wide, several neighboring skin or sky tones may create visible smoothing. At 50 stitches wide, those same shades can turn into confetti. Choose color count together with resolution rather than treating them as independent settings in conversion software.

Check every color in the usage statistics. A shade appearing in only a handful of stitches deserves manual inspection. Sometimes those stitches define a catchlight or important edge and must remain; other times they are noise generated by image sampling. Removing low-value shades is one of the fastest ways to make a converted pattern more pleasant to stitch.

Physical thread matters too. Digital RGB colors do not map perfectly to embroidery floss, and two DMC references that look distinct on screen may be much closer in real thread. For critical palettes, compare actual skeins or a real-thread color card under neutral light before publishing the pattern.

Our PDF key should contain exactly the colors used in the final grid, with no missing or obsolete entries. If we offer a reduced-color edition, it should be a deliberately reviewed version with a new preview and key, not an automatic “fewer colors” export that has never been checked for likeness or contrast.

Color count should also be judged against symbol complexity. A chart with sixty colors needs sixty clearly distinguishable key entries and enough symbol variety to keep neighboring shades readable. If the palette grows faster than the symbol system can support comfortably at print size, that is another signal to simplify.

Thread quantity changes with palette structure. Ten colors used in large blocks may require several skeins, while fifty accent colors may consume only short lengths. Product planning should therefore separate “number of colors” from “amount of thread” and publish both when workload matters.

For custom conversions, we can present two reviewed palette options only when both genuinely preserve the subject—for example, a detailed edition and a simplified edition. The customer should compare previews rather than choose an arbitrary color count before seeing what detail is lost.

Background color can eliminate entire stitched shades. If the fabric already provides the intended dark, cream or neutral field, leaving that region open can reduce both palette and stitch count. The decision should be made before final color reduction because the surrounding thread colors will be perceived against that ground.

For a pattern sold internationally, use stable thread references and avoid describing the palette only with subjective names such as “dusty rose” or “warm gray.” The DMC code is the repeatable instruction; names and swatches are supporting orientation.
